analysis.one_liner: Bans all offshore oil and gas drilling off Florida's coasts and cancels existing leases there.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote; it sat in subcommittee for 18 months until the 102nd Congress ended, with its final entry pointing to the broader energy bill, H.R.776.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently stop the Interior Department from selling or issuing any offshore oil and gas leases in two areas off Florida — the waters south of a line near Tampa and within 100 miles of the entire Florida coast — and cancel every lease already issued there, paying holders of those leases from the U.S. Treasury. It would also bar all drilling activity in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico off Florida until at least 2002, while the Interior Department ran environmental studies of the area. The bill never left its subcommittees and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Florida's coastal communities and the people whose livelihoods depend on clean beaches and healthy Gulf waters: tourism workers, beachfront businesses, commercial and recreational fishing interests, and residents exposed to oil-spill risk. Florida itself would bear no cost — any compensation owed to cancelled leaseholders would come from the federal Treasury.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida coastal towns, tourism, and fishing

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits the Interior Secretary from any leasing or drilling activity in waters off Florida — south of 26°N latitude/east of 86°W longitude and within 100 nautical miles of Florida's coastline [S3].
Cancels all existing federal oil and gas leases in those areas and requires annual reports to Congress on the cancellations until complete [S3].

Bars lease sales, exploration plans, development plans, and drilling permits in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico Planning Area off Florida until at least January 1, 2002, and only after independent scientists review environmental studies [S3].

Requires the Interior Department to conduct ecological, oceanographic, and endangered-species studies of the area before any activity resumes, with $1 million per year authorized for the studies through fiscal 2001 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding leases in the prohibited areas, whose leases would be cancelled; the federal Treasury, which would pay any compensation owed to those leaseholders (Florida pays nothing); and, in a small way, federal taxpayers funding the $1 million annual environmental studies. Consumers could eventually face marginally higher energy costs from reduced Gulf leasing, though any near-term effect is negligible since the areas were not major producing zones.

drawbacks.text: The bill cancels already-issued leases and pays any owed compensation out of the U.S. Treasury, so taxpayers — not Florida — would foot the bill for canceling rights companies had legitimately purchased [S3].

A permanent, geographically absolute prohibition removes those waters from national energy production entirely, rather than setting a precautionary review process that could reopen them if studies showed drilling could be done safely [S3].
The prohibition's end date is open-ended: drilling could resume only after studies completed and reviewed, with no requirement that Florida agree to the restart [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Florida specifically, the protection is large relative to the cost: the state gets oil-spill protection for its beaches and fishing grounds while paying nothing, and taxpayers' main direct cost is compensation to leaseholders plus $1 million a year in studies. The serious costs fall on a concentrated group — leaseholders whose rights are cancelled — and on national energy supply to a minor degree. The permanent cancellation of purchased lease rights without a sunset is the design feature an honest supporter would have to defend.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in subcommittees of two House committees for about 18 months and never reached the floor; its final action entry notes it was superseded by H.R.776, the broader energy bill of that Congress.

narrative.text: Introduced April 9, 1991 by Rep. Dante Fascell with 13 cosponsors (7 Democrats, 6 Republicans) and referred jointly to the Interior and Insular Affairs and Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committees [S1] [S4] [S5].

Within a week it was sent to two subcommittees — Oceanography, Great Lakes, and the Outer Continental Shelf, and Water, Power and Offshore Energy Resources — and executive comments were requested from Commerce, Interior, and EPA [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor action followed; the last action, on October 8, 1992, notes 'See H.R.776' [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993, so the bill died without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies holding leases off Florida came out ahead, because the permanent drilling ban and lease cancellation never became law. Florida's coastal communities got only the partial protection carried in the broader energy bill the House's final action pointed to (H.R.776), not the permanent ban this bill proposed.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but regional rather than partisan — 7 Democrats and 6 Republicans, all Florida members, cosponsored; the record shows no action, and no votes, beyond the Florida delegation's sponsorship [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Oil and gas (offshore leasing and drilling)
industries.note: The bill cancels existing federal leases off Florida and permanently bars new leasing, exploration, and drilling there, converting assets those companies had paid for into Treasury compensation claims. Blocking drilling protects beaches, fishing grounds, and tourism economies from spill risk, which is why the industry's interest runs against coastal residents' here.

Permanently protecting waters within 100 miles of Florida's coast shields the beaches and coastal economies that depend on them from oil-spill risk. These are ordinary people's employers as much as an industry.

Barring drilling in the Eastern Gulf and Florida's offshore waters protects fish habitats and fishing grounds that Gulf drilling activity can disturb. The bill requires endangered-species and marine-mammal surveys in the area [S3].
